The figure summarizes how stem and progenitor cells generate specialized cell types in several tissues, highlighting that each tissue follows a branching lineage from a small pool of less differentiated cells.

In muscle, a muscle progenitor gives rise to myoblasts and satellite cells, and myoblasts fuse into myotubes that then differentiate into fast- or slow-twitch muscle. In blood, hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells branch through intermediate progenitors into lymphoid and myeloid lineages, producing T, NK, and B cells, as well as monocytes, granulocytes, erythrocytes, and platelets.

In skin, an embryonic epidermal cell produces epidermal, hair follicle, and sebaceous gland stem cells. These generate the layered epidermis and the major hair follicle compartments, including matrix cells and inner and outer root sheath structures, showing how one developmental source feeds both surface skin and appendages.

In the nervous system, neuroepithelial stem cells produce radial glial cells, which then generate neurons and glial progenitors. These progenitors form oligodendrocytes and astrocytes, while a neural stem-like intermediate appears capable of producing both neurons and glia. Overall, the image emphasizes hierarchical differentiation and tissue-specific fate restriction.
